title: Gospel of John: The Road to Easter
intro: 47 days through the Gospel of John, from Ash Wednesday to Easter Sunday, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Today is Ash Wednesday, when many Christians receive a cross of ashes on the forehead. In Western churches it begins Lent, the 40 days before Easter, not counting Sundays; Orthodox Easter often falls later. Starting today, 47 days through the Gospel of John, ending at the empty tomb on Easter Sunday. John opens by echoing Genesis 1:1 with a bold claim: the Word (Greek logos), whom he will identify with Jesus, existed before creation, was with God, and was God.

John's opening lines, often called the Prologue, introduce themes that run through his whole book, like light and darkness. The point here is hope: the light is still shining, and the darkness has not put it out. The Greek verb translated "overcome" can also mean "grasp," which is why the King James Version reads "the darkness comprehended it not." Tradition credits this Gospel to the apostle John; many scholars think it was the last of the four written.

The Word who was with God in the beginning now becomes a human being. "Made His dwelling" literally means "pitched His tent" in Greek, recalling the tabernacle, the tent where God's presence dwelt among Israel in the wilderness. Christians call this the Incarnation, from Latin words meaning "in flesh."

John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and points him out with this title. (This Gospel simply calls him John, and its author never gives his own name.) Lambs were offered in the temple every day and eaten at Passover, the festival remembering Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt. Christians read the title as pointing to Jesus' death, which they believe takes away the sin of the world. That Passover image returns at the end of John's story.

Philip tells Nathanael that they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about: Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael is skeptical, since Nazareth was a small village in Galilee, never mentioned in the Hebrew scriptures. Philip doesn't argue; he invites him to meet Jesus and see for himself. "Come and see" repeats Jesus' own invitation a few verses earlier, and in John, faith often begins with an encounter like this.

At a wedding in Cana in Galilee, the wine runs out, an embarrassment for the hosts. Jesus' mother, never named in John's Gospel, tells him, and then tells the servants this, trusting him to act. At his word, six stone jars of 20 to 30 gallons each are filled with water, which becomes better wine than what was served first. John calls it the first of Jesus' "signs": acts that point to who he is.

Jesus has driven the merchants and money changers out of the temple courts, and the authorities demand a sign to prove his authority. His answer sounds absurd, since the temple took forty-six years to build, but John explains that Jesus meant his own body, which would be killed and raised. Mark places the temple scene in Jesus' last week; John puts it near the start, and scholars debate whether it happened twice or John arranged his story by theme.

Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader among his people, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one can see God's kingdom without a completely new start, a birth that comes from God. The Greek word translated "again," anothen, can also mean "from above." Nicodemus hears only the first meaning and asks how a grown man could be born a second time. He appears only in John, and he will be back.

Jesus is still answering Nicodemus, who can't see how anyone could be born again. He uses a play on words: in Greek, pneuma means both "wind" and "spirit," and so does the Hebrew ruach. The point is that the Spirit's work is real but can't be controlled or fully explained: like the wind, it can't be seen, only heard, and known by what it does.

Often called the best-known verse in the Bible, and many Christians see it as the gospel in one sentence: God's love for the world is shown by giving his Son, so that anyone who believes may have eternal life. The Greek word translated "so" mainly means "in this way," pointing to how God loved. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, so translations differ on whether these are still Jesus' words to Nicodemus or the Gospel writer's reflection.

John the Baptist's followers are worried that the crowds are now going to Jesus instead. John compares himself to the friend of the bridegroom, something like a best man, glad to step aside. Augustine later tied this verse to the calendar: the Baptist's birth is celebrated in June, as days begin to shorten, and Jesus' in December, as they begin to lengthen.

Passing through Samaria, a tired Jesus sits by Jacob's well around noon and asks a local woman for a drink. Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility over who were Israel's true heirs and where God should be worshiped, Jerusalem or Mount Gerizim in Samaria. A Jewish teacher asking a Samaritan woman for a drink crossed two lines at once.

At the well, Jesus has offered the Samaritan woman "living water," everyday speech for fresh water from a spring. She takes him literally, so he explains: he means something that satisfies a deeper thirst, a life from God that keeps welling up inside a person. The prophet Jeremiah had called God "the fountain of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13), an image Jesus' listeners may have recognized.

Jesus has told the woman things about her past, and says plainly that he is the Messiah. She leaves her water jar and goes back to town, inviting people to come and see for themselves. The outsider becomes a messenger: many there come to believe, calling him "the Savior of the world." Eastern Orthodox tradition gives her the name Photini, "the enlightened one," and honors her as a saint.

Back in Cana, a royal official, probably in the service of Herod Antipas, begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son in Capernaum. Jesus sends him home with only a promise, and the point is the man's trust: he believes Jesus' word without seeing anything. On the way, his servants meet him with news that the boy recovered at the very hour Jesus spoke. John counts this as the second sign.

At a feast in Jerusalem, Jesus meets a man who has been an invalid for 38 years, lying by the Pool of Bethesda. The question sounds obvious, but the man doesn't say yes; he explains why he can't get well: no one helps him into the water when it is stirred. Jesus bypasses the pool and heals him with a word. Archaeologists have uncovered a large double pool near St. Anne's Church in Jerusalem that many identify as this one.

Criticized for healing on the Sabbath and calling God his own Father, Jesus answers with a long speech. Here he makes a striking promise: whoever hears his word and trusts the God who sent him already has eternal life, not only after death but starting now. "Truly, truly" is the Hebrew word amen said twice; only John doubles it, about 25 times, to mark an especially solemn statement.

A huge crowd has followed Jesus, and he asks where they could buy bread for everyone. Andrew points out a boy's lunch, then doubts it's worth mentioning. The point is in that doubt: what seems hopelessly small is what Jesus uses to feed five thousand. Only John mentions the boy, and that his loaves were barley, the cheaper bread of ordinary people. Apart from the resurrection, this is the only miracle told in all four Gospels.

That night the disciples are rowing across the Sea of Galilee in a strong wind when they see Jesus walking toward them on the water. "It is I" is literally "I am" in Greek, ego eimi. Many readers hear an echo of the name God gave Moses at the burning bush: "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14).

The day after the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd asks for a sign like the manna, the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness. Jesus answers that he himself is the bread they need, satisfying a deeper hunger than ordinary food can. This is the first of seven "I am" sayings in John, each pairing "I am" with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, and vine.

After the bread of life teaching, many followers find it too hard to accept and leave. Jesus asks the Twelve whether they want to go too, and Peter answers for them: even if they don't understand everything, there is no one else to turn to. Many scholars see this as John's counterpart to Peter's declaration in Mark 8, "You are the Christ."

Jesus has come to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles, though John notes that even his own brothers did not believe in him. Teaching in the temple, he defends his Sabbath healing: boys were circumcised on the Sabbath when their eighth day fell on it, so why object to making a whole person well? His conclusion is a call to look past appearances and judge by what is actually right.

Tabernacles was the autumn harvest festival, when people lived in temporary shelters to remember Israel's years in the wilderness. According to the Mishnah, priests poured water from the Pool of Siloam at the temple altar each day of the feast. On the last and greatest day, Jesus offers himself as the source of living water for anyone who is thirsty, and John explains that he meant the Spirit. Many scholars think he was playing on that ritual.

The chief priests and Pharisees had sent temple officers to arrest Jesus. They come back empty-handed, and this is their explanation: they were so struck by his words that they couldn't bring themselves to seize him. Then Nicodemus, the Pharisee who once visited Jesus at night, speaks up, asking whether their law condemns a man without first hearing him.

Religious leaders bring a woman caught in adultery and ask whether she should be stoned, hoping to trap Jesus. He turns the question back on them: only someone without sin should throw the first stone. One by one they leave, and Jesus tells her he does not condemn her either; she should go and sin no more. The oldest manuscripts of John lack this story, so many Bibles bracket it; many scholars think it's an early story about Jesus that copyists added later.

Teaching in the temple near the treasury, Jesus makes the second of John's "I am" sayings: following him means walking in light, not darkness, with a light that gives life. The Mishnah describes giant lamps lit in that part of the temple during the Feast of Tabernacles, bright enough to light up all of Jerusalem. Many scholars think Jesus' words play on that setting.

Jesus is teaching in the temple, speaking to people who have begun to believe him. He tells them that real discipleship means holding on to his teaching, and that knowing the truth brings freedom. They object that, as Abraham's descendants, they have never been anyone's slaves, and he explains that he means slavery to sin. The line about truth is carved in the lobby of CIA headquarters, and in Latin it is the motto of Johns Hopkins University.

The argument about Abraham ends here. Jesus says "I am," not "I was," and many readers hear God's name from Exodus 3:14 once more. The crowd seems to take it as a claim to be divine: in the next verse they pick up stones to throw at him, the penalty for blasphemy in the law of Moses.

Seeing a man blind from birth, the disciples ask whose sin caused it, a common assumption at the time. Jesus answers that neither the man nor his parents sinned, then puts mud on his eyes and sends him to wash. The man simply obeys, and comes back seeing. John translates the pool's name, "Sent," which many readers connect with Jesus as the one sent by God. Steps of this pool from Jesus' time were uncovered in 2004.

Religious leaders question the healed man, insisting that Jesus is a sinner for healing on the Sabbath. He sticks to what he knows, and they end up throwing him out. John Newton, a former slave-ship captain, echoed this line in his hymn "Amazing Grace": "was blind, but now I see."

Jesus is speaking to the leaders who threw out the man he had healed of blindness. He contrasts a thief, who comes only to take, with his own purpose: to give people life in all its fullness. "Fullness" translates a Greek word for abundance, more than enough; the King James Version has "more abundantly." Chapter numbers date only from the 1200s, so this speech follows straight on from that scene.

The fourth "I am" saying. What makes this shepherd good is that he will die for his sheep, rather than run from danger the way a hired hand does. Christians read it as pointing to Jesus' death. In the Hebrew scriptures, God is Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23), and the prophet Ezekiel condemned leaders who fed themselves instead of the flock. Some of the earliest Christian art, in Rome's catacombs, shows Jesus as a shepherd carrying a sheep.

It's winter, and Jesus is at the temple for the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah, which marks the temple's rededication around 164 BC after the Greek king Antiochus IV defiled it. Asked to say plainly whether he is the Messiah, Jesus answers with this. The crowd hears a claim to be God and picks up stones again; Christians read it as a central statement of Jesus' unity with the Father.

Word came that Jesus' friend Lazarus was sick in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, yet Jesus waited two days before setting out. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. His sister Martha meets Jesus with these words, part grief and part reproach, and then, in the next verse, faith: even now, God will give him whatever he asks. Her sister Mary later greets Jesus with the very same words.

Jesus tells Martha that her brother will rise again, and she answers that she knows he will, in the resurrection at the end of time. Jesus moves that hope into the present: resurrection and life are found in him, and death is not the end for those who trust him. This is the fifth "I am" saying. These words open the funeral service in the Book of Common Prayer and are read at many Christian funerals.

The shortest verse in most English Bibles. Mary has fallen at Jesus' feet weeping, and the mourners with her are wailing. For Jesus, John switches to a different Greek word, one that means shedding tears rather than loud mourning. He grieves even though, in John's telling, he is about to raise Lazarus.

Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and Martha warns about the smell when Jesus asks for the stone to be removed. After a prayer, Jesus calls out, and the dead man walks out wrapped in burial cloths. It is the climax of Jesus' signs in John, showing his power over death itself. Eastern Orthodox churches remember this story on Lazarus Saturday, the day before Palm Sunday.

News of Lazarus reaches the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, which fears a popular movement will bring Roman force down on the nation. The high priest Caiaphas offers this cold calculation: better that one man die than the whole nation. John sees an irony in it, an unintended prophecy that Jesus would die for the nation and for God's scattered children. From then on, the council plots his death; in Mark, that plot follows the temple scene instead.

Six days before Passover, Jesus is back in Bethany at a dinner with Martha, Mary and Lazarus. Mary pours costly perfume on his feet, an act of extravagant love. When Judas complains it was worth 300 denarii, about a year's wages, Jesus says she has kept it for the day of his burial. Mark tells a similar story about an unnamed woman. In John, the next day is the entry into Jerusalem, and tomorrow is Palm Sunday.

Today is Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week. Crowds in Jerusalem for Passover go out to welcome Jesus as their king, waving palm branches, a symbol of victory, as he rides in on a young donkey. "Hosanna" is Hebrew for "save, please," from Psalm 118, and their shouts express the hope that he is the one to save them. Only John mentions palms, which is where this Sunday gets its name.

Monday of Holy Week. Some Greeks who have come for Passover ask to see Jesus, and he replies that the hour has come. All through John, his "hour" had not yet come; now it has, and he describes his death with the image of a seed, which yields a harvest only after it is buried. Christians read this as his death bringing life to many. Dostoevsky chose this verse as the epigraph for The Brothers Karamazov.

Tuesday of Holy Week. John 13 to 17 is Jesus' long farewell to his disciples on his last evening, and this plan reads from it through Thursday, saving the foot washing that opens it for last. Jesus has said he is going to prepare a place for them, and Thomas asks how they can know the way. Jesus answers that he himself is the way to the Father: the sixth "I am" saying. The earliest Christians called their movement "the Way."

Wednesday of Holy Week, known in some traditions as Spy Wednesday, recalling Judas' secret deal to betray Jesus. In his farewell, Jesus has called himself the true vine, the last "I am" saying, and told his disciples to love one another as he has loved them. This verse names the greatest love, giving your life for your friends, which he is about to do. It is carved on many war memorials.

Today is Maundy Thursday, the night John 13 to 17 took place, so the plan steps back to how that evening began. Instead of describing the bread and cup, John tells how Jesus washed his disciples' feet, a task usually left to servants. The point is that their Lord and Teacher took the lowest place, and they should serve each other the same way. "Maundy" comes from the Latin mandatum, "commandment," after the new commandment he gives that night: love one another.

Today is Good Friday, when Christians remember the crucifixion. Jesus' last word in John is a single Greek word, tetelestai: finished, completed, accomplished. Christians read it not as defeat but as the completion of his mission. In Mark the Last Supper is a Passover meal, but in John, Jesus dies on the day before Passover, the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, recalling John the Baptist's words: "Look, the Lamb of God."

Today is Holy Saturday, the quiet day between the cross and Easter. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who first came to Jesus by night, wrap his body in linen with about 75 pounds of myrrh and aloes, a lavish amount. With the Sabbath about to begin, they lay him in this nearby tomb. Many churches hold an Easter Vigil after dark tonight.

Today is Easter Sunday. Weeping outside the empty tomb, Mary Magdalene mistakes Jesus for the gardener until he says her name. Because she is the first to announce the resurrection, Christian tradition calls her the "apostle to the apostles." That's the road to Easter through the Gospel of John. Thank you for walking it with me.
